story_text.value:
I asked 12 different AI models to build the HTML to fill its own tank at an aquarium — then displayed them for you to see and vote on your favorite one! I did this for several other "gallery" themes, such as fungi, fairy cards, bonsai trees, and constellations.

Maybe not surprising, but it was interesting to see how often the models converged. Certain archetypes, such as moths or cranes in the "planetarium" gallery, appear frequently, not just in the same model family but also across model families. In the aquarium, I counted two cuttlefish, two octopuses, and two puffers (out of all of the fish in the sea!!).

You might also notice particular themes or tendencies appear for certain models - for example, is it just me, or does Muse Wonder feel extremely ADHD or what? (look at the apothecary and fungarium in particular)

Everyone is buying a Mac Mini for their agents, or better, giving them a Linux box (see https://x.com/theo/status/2090528543746965991).

I found this quite tedious to setup every time, so I built a "custom" nixOS image to create a repeatable and customizable computer for my agents. It takes ~5 minutes to install, has a sleek-ish dashboard, and is fully open-source.

You could set this up yourself, but for setting up agent multiplexers like T3 Code I find this pretty easy / nice.

Check it out. It's very early, so LMK if you run into any issues.

:)

story_text.value:
Hey Everyone, Andrej here, I wanted to showcase a small service that I built for automatically transferring invoices from Cliniko to QuickBooks. I don't believe that such a service yet exists so if you or somebody you know uses both Cliniko and QuickBooks to manage their small medical practice, there's a high chance there could be some benefit from this service.

It has a free tier as well as a sandbox which can be tested and played around with at sandbox.invoice-funnel.com. You would need to have both a Cliniko account to create invoices and a QuickBooks account to see them land in case you want to try it out.

Even if you don't use Cliniko or have never heard of it, any general comments/questions or accounting-specific tips would be greatly appreciated!

P.S. Currently this service supports only Cliniko, but if you know of any other app that generates invoices, has a public API and currently no or limited integration with QuickBooks, please do let me know and I can consider on-boarding it.

Thanks for your attention!

story_text.value:
Howdy!

I've been working on an open-source tool that helps lighten the burden of reviewing what your coding agents write. You still see all the lines of code, but the agents write a "tour guide" that links you through the local PR, and as you have questions or comments, you chat with your agent in the context of the code, in a threaded conversation.

I called it "gavel" (you make your agents build a case that you judge). Hope you find it as useful as I do!

https://github.com/photostructure/gavel

story_text.value:
Hi everyone!

Installing skills globally in ~/.agents or ~/.claude consumes too much context, yet manually installing specific skills for every project is tedious. Wouldn't it be better to group skills for programming, backend architecture, or graphic design into collections, and install them with a single command only when needed?

To solve this, I built Skillset. It acts as a wrapper around the Vercel Skill CLI that batch-installs sets of skills from multiple sources using a single JSON file, essentially npm for skills!

While similar tools exist, most are written from scratch, which makes me concerned about their compatibility. Because Vercel’s Skill CLI is already the de facto standard (imo!), Skillset uses it directly as an underlying library. So it guarantees seamless compatibility across teams, regardless of whether they use Skillset or the standard Vercel CLI.

title.value: Show HN: Skillset: Easily curate and install agent skills collection

story_text.value:
rbit is a self hosted git forge designed around three core philosophies: speed, security, and efficiency.

We built rbit using Rust, Axum, Askama, Gitoxide, SQLite + redb, HTMX + Tailwind. Every piece of the stack was carefully considered to provide users with the fastest possible experience working with their repos without sacrificing the functionality you've come to expect from your existing git forge.

Our team is actively working to help make rbit the best it can be and we'd love to get your feedback while we continue improving!

rbit is built using rbit and it's CI/CD pipeline, we are dogfooding as we build it in the open. It has been localized into 9 languages including: English, Spanish, Portuguese, French, German, Russian, Chinese (Simplified), Japanese, and Korean. If you're a native speaker we would happily accept translation fixes!

story_text.value:
My mom is a photographer and an artist. This year, she complained that she doesn't quite enjoy the existing options for storing, sharing, and organizing her work.

After a few sessions, I think we got into the ballpark of what it should look like if we weren't Google or SmugMug: with a host of extra features (clutter detection, decent search, book and album writing, even calorie and activity tracking, and a few other conveniences)

The original intention was to build an application that would serve our family. But I feel like it's growing into something bigger as people are joining in. If you want to try, here's an invite code (capped at 50 signups): YRASHK-7ZXA-S3K3-DM8V

story_text.value:
I've long thought about how we're influenced by CPU architectures, and importantly, their ISAs.

In a discussion at a meetup, I brought up a topic that interested me for a while: how would an ISA that exposes memory and cache interactions in a more explicit way (because if you think about it, memory is very much I/O), as opposed to being smart and predictive on its own?

An obscure interest, of course. Nevertheless, I wanted to build a quick prototype after that.

What ended up transpiring was a bit larger. A multicore architecture with tiered stores, capabilities, a JIT'd emulator, Verilog RTL with a simulator, a small microkernel OS, UI, JIT Forth, an assembler in its own assembly, a bootstrapping C99 compiler, a few games, a visual debugger, and a few other things.

(This also shows just how far a directed LLM process can go in little time)

title.value: Show HN: Strata Architecture

story_text.value:
I've seen too many slow-log queries with a GROUP BY that makes Postgres blow up, so for the last two weeks or so I've been working on Straum. You declare the aggregates as a view, and Straum answers over HTTP (other transports might be added). I've been using the New York taxi dataset as a benchmark. On the heavier GROUP BYs I see about 1,000x to 5,000x. It's written in Rust (of course).

It leans on Postgres replication slots, logical or physical, to get its data. Postgres stays the source of truth.

What do you think?

Benchmark: https://janbjorge.github.io/straum/benchmark.html Repo: https://github.com/janbjorge/straum
